soil-water-029.title: Aeolian processes: how wind moves the land
soil-water-029.text: Wind carries minerals from the Sahara all the way to the Amazon basin, and Saharan dust has built red clay soils in southern Europe. That long haul is the work of aeolian processes: the erosion, transport and deposition of sediment by wind at or near the Earth's surface. The name comes from Aeolus, the Greek god who kept the winds. Worldwide, water erodes more than wind does. Yet wind matters greatly in arid and semi-arid regions such as deserts. It works best where plants are sparse, the soil is dry and loose {{ref:soil-water-046}} lies ready. Wind is also a sorter. It separates sand from silt and clay, heaping sand into sandy deposits called ergs and laying silty loess farther from the source. Grains colliding in the air chip at one another, a process called attrition. It rounds and frosts sand grains and is a major source of dust 2–5 microns across. Wind deposits are not confined to dry lands. They also form along shorelines and on glacial outwash, and much of North America and Europe rests on windblown sand and loess from the Pleistocene.

soil-water-051.title: Sediment control: keeping a building site's soil at home
soil-water-051.text: In 1965 Montgomery County, Maryland, began the first local government program to keep construction soil out of its waters. Maryland followed with a statewide program in 1970. Sediment control is any practice or device that holds eroded soil on a construction site so it does not wash off and pollute nearby waters. It usually works alongside {{ref:soil-water-050}}, which stops soil moving in the first place and so lightens the load on sediment controls. The common tools include fabric fences, settling ponds and traps, rolls of fiber, straw bale and sand bag barriers, storm drain inlet protection and turbidity curtains. Most are temporary, though some also serve for stormwater management. Every U.S. state requires these controls on construction sites above a set size, and federal rules apply from 1 acre (0.40 ha). They must go in before clearing and grading begin and stay maintained until the disturbance ends.

soil-water-018.title: When eroded soil becomes the river's pollutant
soil-water-018.text: Each year the Yellow River carries over 1.6 billion tons of sediment to the ocean, most of it washed off the Loess Plateau by water erosion. Soil erosion, especially from farmland, is considered the leading global cause of diffuse water pollution. Sediment harms waters in its own right. Silt fills the gaps between gravel where fish spawn, cuts their food supply and clogs their gills, and the variety of plants, algae and invertebrates declines. Eroded soil also carries attached pesticides and heavy metals, plus fertilizers that overfeed rivers with nutrients. On Madagascar's central plateau, gullies called lavakas may supply 84% of river sediment, turning rivers dark red-brown and killing fish. Near coral reefs, sediment from watershed development smothers and scrapes the corals and feeds algal blooms. Removing an estimated 135 million m3 of eroded sediment likely costs the EU and UK over 2.3 billion euros a year.

soil-water-053.title: Mass wasting: when gravity alone moves the ground
soil-water-053.text: Some soil leaves a hillside with no river, wind or ice to carry it. Mass wasting, also called mass movement, is the movement of rock or soil down slopes under the force of gravity. Unlike other erosion, the moving debris travels in no medium at all. Water usually aids it without being the carrier. With more water, a sliding mass grows ever more fluid, grading through flows of debris and mud and finally into sheetfloods. The forms range from slow creep of the soil to sudden rockfalls, acting over seconds to hundreds of years. Broadly, movements are either creeps or slides, described in {{ref:soil-water-055}} and {{ref:soil-water-057}}, and subsidence is sometimes counted as well. In mountains it is often the first stage in moving weathered material, carrying it down to where streams and glaciers can pick it up. Weak, unconsolidated material, steep slopes, freeze-thaw, heavy rain and undercutting by digging or erosion all promote it. Speed decides the damage. Slow creep deforms roads and breaks pipelines, while rapid slides can be deadly. Walls, catchment dams for rockfall and debris, tree planting, better drainage of source areas and {{ref:soil-water-065}} all reduce the threat.

soil-water-064.title: Slope stability: the balance between strength and stress
soil-water-064.text: Whether a hillside stands or slides comes down to a single ratio. Slope stability is the ability of a soil or rock slope to withstand movement; its opposite is slope instability, or slope failure. Engineers express it as a safety factor: the available {{ref:soil-phys-101}} divided by the shear stress acting along a possible sliding surface. A slope is stable overall if that factor exceeds 1 on every possible surface from top to toe, and the smallest value speaks for the whole slope. Values between about 1 and 1.3 mark slopes that need watching or strengthening. Intense rain, snowmelt, earthquakes, toe erosion, building loads, road cuts and {{ref:soil-water-100}} can all trigger failure. After heavy rain, pore water pressure on the slip surface lowers the {{ref:soil-phys-100}} and the friction, while the added groundwater makes the soil heavier. A little moisture can steady a slope, but saturation acts as a lubricant. Pure clay often fails along a near-circular surface, while slab-shaped slips strip a layer of soil off the bedrock.

soil-water-057.title: Landslides: when a slope's strength gives way
soil-water-057.text: A landslide can strike a mountain, a coastal cliff, a gentle slope or the seafloor. The word covers several forms of {{ref:soil-water-053}} with relatively rapid ground movement, including rockfalls, slope failures and fast flows of mud and debris. Gravity drives them all. A slope fails when the shear strength of its material falls, the shear stress on it rises, or both, the balance set out in {{ref:soil-water-064}}. Many slides follow a specific event such as heavy rain, an earthquake or a road cut, though the trigger is not always identifiable. Natural causes include wetting and rising pore water pressure, undercutting by rivers or waves, weathering and earthquake shaking. Wildfire adds another, by destroying vegetation and soil structure. People aggravate slides through deforestation, cultivation, construction and earthworks. Removing deep-rooted plants that bind loose slope debris to bedrock does the same. Degraded land loosens the grip of plants on soil, and with extreme rainfall it makes erosion and landslides more frequent. Saturated material can turn into a flowing mass that carries off trees, houses and cars and blocks rivers. Landslides under water or into water can generate tsunamis.

soil-water-055.title: Soil creep: the slope that moves while no one watches
soil-water-055.text: In old churchyards, headstones lean and sit metres from where they were set. The ground beneath them has been moving. Downhill creep, or soil creep, is the slow downward movement of soil and rock on a gentle slope. It looks continuous but is the sum of many tiny, separate movements driven by gravity, and the steeper the slope, the faster it goes. Friction holds slope material in place. As a slope steepens, less of gravity's pull presses into it, so friction falls. Water cuts both ways. A little gives soil cohesion, like damp sand in a sandcastle, but saturation fills the pores and creates a slip plane. Clay that swells when wet pushes soil downhill and settles at its new position as it dries. Freeze-thaw and heating-cooling cycles ratchet soil down the same way. Trees grow curved and fences tilt as the soil carries them along. Plant roots bind loose material and draw off excess water, though they add weight, so bare slopes are more likely to move. Creep deforms roads and breaks pipelines, so engineers drive pilings deep enough to keep it from undermining foundations. Modelled as a slow diffusion of {{ref:soil-form-097}}, creep rounds off ridges over long timescales.

soil-water-047.title: Reading a sand grain's travels from its shape
soil-water-047.text: A frosted sand grain is a strong hint that the wind once carried it. Sediment grain shape describes particles by three parameters: overall form, or sphericity, the roundness of corners, and surface texture. Form is spherical, platy or rodlike, worked out from the lengths of a grain's long, intermediate and short axes with formulas such as Krumbein's or Sneed and Folk's. Roundness runs from very angular to very rounded and is usually judged against comparison charts. Pits, fractures and scratches on the surface, studied mostly on quartz grains under an electron microscope, reveal how a grain traveled.

soil-water-008.title: Chemical erosion: landscapes carried off in solution
soil-water-008.text: A sinkhole is erosion with no solid debris to show for it. Chemical erosion is the loss of material from a landscape in dissolved form, as solutes. Physical erosion, by contrast, removes rock or soil as solid particles of sediment. Because the material leaves in solution, chemical erosion is usually calculated from the dissolved load that streams carry. Sinkholes and other karst features are its extreme example. Anders Rapp pioneered its study in work on Kärkevagge, published in 1960.

soil-water-007.title: Coastal erosion: waves against the shore
soil-water-007.text: A wave's most effective weapon is the sediment it carries. Coastal erosion is the wearing away of shorelines, mainly by currents and waves, with changes in sea level also playing a part. Waves work by hydraulic action, pounding, corrosion of rock such as limestone by carbonic acid, and attrition of their own load. Abrasion, or corrasion, in which waves hurl sediment at cliffs, is the fastest and most effective. Longshore drift moves sediment along the coast, and erosion occurs where less arrives from upcurrent than is carried away. Sea-level rise caused by climate change has greatly increased coastal erosion rates.

soil-water-009.title: Glacial erosion: ice that sandpapers whole valleys
soil-water-009.text: A U-shaped valley takes an estimated 100,000 years to carve. Glacial erosion is the work of moving glacier ice, mainly through abrasion, plucking and ice thrusting. In abrasion, debris frozen into the base of the ice scrapes, polishes and gouges the bed like sandpaper on wood. In plucking, the glacier breaks off pieces of bedrock. In ice thrusting, a glacier frozen to its bed carries large sheets of frozen sediment forward as it surges. Ice and meltwater leave moraines, drumlins, ground moraine, kames and glacial erratics behind.

soil-water-006.title: How rivers cut their valleys down and out
soil-water-006.text: Most of a river's erosion happens during floods. River and stream erosion is the work of water flowing continuously along a channel, deepening valleys and wearing away banks. It cuts downward and also headward into the hillside, leaving head cuts and steep banks. Early on it works mostly downward, carving V-shaped valleys. Once the stream reaches a base level, erosion turns sideways and widens the valley floor. Pebbles and boulders dragged along the bed abrade it, a process called traction. Bank erosion, distinct from scour of the bed, rises sharply with heavier runoff from built-up land.

soil-water-048.title: Sediment transport: how water, wind and ice move the pieces
soil-water-048.text: Every grain on a riverbed, from clay to boulder, waits for a flow strong enough to move it. Sediment transport is the movement of solid particles by gravity together with the water, air or ice that carries them. Its study mostly serves prediction: whether erosion or deposition will happen, how much, and over what time and distance. The physics is a contest. Stronger flows raise the lift and drag on a particle, while larger or denser particles tend to fall out. Water moves bigger grains than air because it is denser and more viscous. Rivers usually carry sand and gravel, and big floods shift cobbles and boulders. Moving water shapes ripples, river patterns and the flat ground beside channels by eroding and depositing on its bed. Wind moves fine sediment and builds soils from airborne dust, while glaciers carry a wide range of sizes and drop them in moraines. Changes in flow power decide where material is lost or gained. Locally that happens behind boulders and inside meanders, and regionally after a dam is built or removed. On hillslopes, soil creep, falling trees, burrowing animals and landslides move {{ref:soil-form-097}} downslope, and erosion rates climb steeply as slopes near the angle of repose. When human activity loads a river with enough fine material to fill its channels, the problem is called siltation.

soil-water-049.title: How much eroded soil actually reaches the river
soil-water-049.text: In Europe, only about 15% of eroded soil is expected to reach a river outlet. That share is the sediment delivery ratio: the fraction of gross erosion on a catchment, counting interrill, rill, gully and stream erosion, that arrives at the outlet. The rest is deposited along the way. Sediment distribution models such as WaTEM/SEDEM simulate where material is moved and where it settles, and the European figure comes from them. The share that does arrive still brings management and siltation costs to river basins.

soil-water-056.title: Solifluction: soil that creeps over frozen ground
soil-water-056.text: In 1906 Johan Gunnar Andersson coined the word solifluction for water-saturated debris moving in periglacial regions. Such slow movements were later tied to freezing and thawing instead. Solifluction now means gradual downslope mass movement of soil linked to that cycle. It is typical of arctic and alpine climates, where soil thawed and saturated in summer creeps down moderate, sparsely vegetated slopes over {{ref:soil-env-129}}. It is slow but widespread, building tongue-shaped lobes and sheets of poorly layered debris. Because it needs cold, humid conditions, it is used to infer past climates.

soil-water-071.title: Quick clay: solid ground that turns to liquid
soil-water-071.text: Some clay stands as firm ground until a shock turns it into a watery fluid. Quick clay, also called Leda or Champlain Sea clay, is a highly sensitive glaciomarine clay. It consists of very fine silt and clay-sized particles ground up by glaciers and first laid down in the sea. Its particle structure is highly unstable, so once remolded it keeps far less strength than it had on first loading. It is found only in lands near the North Pole glaciated in the Pleistocene: Russia, Canada, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Alaska. In Canada it lies mainly in the Ottawa Valley, the St. Lawrence Valley and the Saguenay River region. Earthquake vibrations or massive rainfall can liquefy it suddenly and set off landslides. In Canada alone, quick clay it is linked to more than 250 mapped landslides. Liquefaction, described in {{ref:soil-phys-116}}, usually affects sandy or non-plastic silty soils, so quick clay is one of the rare cases in clay. Known deposits are now commonly tested before any major development.

soil-water-100.title: Internal erosion: the hidden threat inside dams
soil-water-100.text: About half of all embankment dam failures come from water quietly carrying soil away from the inside. Internal erosion is the formation of voids inside a soil as seeping water removes material. It happens when seepage through the pores and cracks of a dam or its foundation exerts enough hydraulic force to detach particles and carry them out. It is also the second most common cause of levee failure. The danger lies in how little shows. Often the only sign is a sand boil, which may be hidden under water, and a dam can breach within hours of the evidence becoming obvious. Piping is its progressive growth, eroding back from the downstream exit until a continuous pipe discharges water. Four types are recognised: a concentrated leak through a crack, backward erosion from the exit point, suffusion and contact erosion. In suffusion, fines wash through the pores between coarse grains that carry most of the {{ref:soil-phys-100}}. Widely or gap-graded cohesionless soils prone to it are called internally unstable. Contact erosion works along an interface between fine and coarse soil. Filters are the defense: layers coarser and more permeable than the soil, which pass seepage but trap eroded particles. They must be internally stable, non-cohesive, free-draining and strong. The critical shear stress that starts a concentrated leak can be estimated with the jet erosion test or the {{ref:soil-water-094}}.

soil-water-252.title: Debris flows: rivers of rock and mud
soil-water-252.text: In 1985 debris flows killed more than 20,000 people at Armero, Colombia. In 1999 they killed tens of thousands in Vargas State, Venezuela. A debris flow is a water-laden mass of soil and broken rock that rushes down mountainsides, funnels into channels and leaves thick muddy deposits on valley floors. Its bulk density is about 2000 kilograms per cubic meter, like other landslides. Yet high {{ref:soil-phys-098}} liquefies the sediment, so it flows almost like water. Sediment fills more than about 40 to 50% of its volume. Floods with about 10 to 40% solids are hyperconcentrated floods instead, and a true {{ref:soil-water-060}} is mostly finer than sand. Three things set one up: slopes steeper than about 25 degrees, plenty of loose sediment, soil or weathered rock, and enough water to almost fully saturate it. Intense rain or snowmelt, dam-break or glacial outburst floods and landslides can trigger them, and they become more frequent after forest and brush fires. In steep channels they often exceed 10 m/s (36 km/h), and flows of up to about 100,000 cubic meters are common in mountains. A boulder-rich head leads a liquefied body of finer sediment. The deposits are poorly sorted lobes edged with boulder levees. Debris basins can catch them, but they are a costly last resort that needs yearly maintenance.

soil-water-032.title: Three ways the wind moves grains
soil-water-032.text: Wind moves sediment in three ways: suspension, short skipping hops described in {{ref:soil-water-251}}, and creep, a rolling or sliding along the ground. Grains start moving at the fluid threshold wind speed, and impacts keep them moving until the wind drops below a lower threshold, a lag called hysteresis. Turbulence lets wind carry grains under 0.05 mm far from coarser ones. Hops matter most for grains up to 2 mm, and landing grains shove heavier ones along as creep, up to 25% of grain movement in deserts. A plant cover of just 15% stops most sand movement.

soil-water-030.title: Deflation: wind that scoops out the desert
soil-water-030.text: Some hollows scoured by wind in Mongolia are 8 km across and 60 to 100 m deep. Deflation is the lifting and removal of loose surface material by turbulent wind. It works through surface creep, suspension and grains bouncing along in short hops, and the hops likely account for 50–70% of it. The hollows it digs, called blowouts, range from dimples 0.3 m deep to those Mongolian giants. Once the fines are gone, a sheet of rock fragments is left behind, the {{ref:soil-water-253}} that floors most deflation zones and shields the material below.

soil-water-033.title: Sand dunes: hills the wind builds
soil-water-033.text: Ralph Bagnold gave the barchan and the linear seif dune their names. A sand dune is a mound or ridge of sediment heaped up by the wind, independent of any obstacle. Its windward slope is gentle, and its downwind side is a steep avalanche slope called the slipface. Under one prevailing wind, transverse dunes form, such as crescent-shaped barchans. Linear dunes run for tens of kilometres, and star dunes have more than two slipfaces. Where plant patches meet active sand such as blowouts, vegetated parabolic dunes form, crescents whose ends point upwind. John Tilton Hack added these in 1941.
